subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The quark composition of a neutron is:
questions.explain: A neutron is one up quark and two down quarks (udd).

questions.q: For a body in rotational equilibrium, the principle of moments states that:
options: Sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments about any point
questions.explain: In equilibrium the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment about any point.

questions.q: A ball of mass 0.20 kg falls 5.0 m from rest. Ignoring air resistance, its kinetic energy just before impact is: (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
questions.explain: KE gained = loss in GPE = mgh = 0.20×9.8×5.0 = 9.8 J.

questions.q: Which is a typical product set of uranium-235 induced fission?
options: Two lighter daughter nuclei plus two or three neutrons
Two equal helium nuclei and no neutrons
questions.explain: U-235 fission produces two unequal daughter nuclei plus 2-3 neutrons and energy.

questions.q: For an object in complete equilibrium under several forces:
options: The resultant force is zero and the resultant moment is zero
The forces must all be equal
questions.explain: Equilibrium requires both zero resultant force and zero resultant moment.

questions.q: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at right angles to each other. The magnitude of the resultant is:
questions.explain: For perpendicular vectors the resultant is √(3²+4²) = 5 N.

questions.q: Which particle has the greatest specific charge?
questions.explain: The electron has a tiny mass yet carries one elementary charge, giving it the largest charge-to-mass ratio.

questions.q: Alpha radiation is typically stopped by:
options: a few cm of air or paper
questions.explain: Alpha particles are absorbed by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air.

questions.q: The electron lepton number of an electron neutrino is:
questions.explain: The electron neutrino, like the electron, has electron lepton number +1.

questions.q: Which radiation is the most penetrating?
questions.explain: Gamma rays are highly penetrating, requiring thick lead or concrete to attenuate.

questions.q: A uniform 2.0 m beam weighs 40 N. Where does its weight effectively act?
options: At its centre, 1.0 m from each end
questions.explain: The weight of a uniform beam acts at its centre of mass, the geometric centre.

questions.q: A sample has a half-life of 8 days. What fraction remains after 24 days?
questions.explain: 24 days is three half-lives, so (1/2)^3 = 1/8 of the sample remains.

questions.q: The relationship between half-life T-half and decay constant lambda is:
questions.explain: Setting N = N0/2 in the decay law gives T-half = ln2/lambda.

questions.q: The specific charge of a particle is defined as its:
questions.explain: Specific charge is the ratio of charge to mass (C/kg).

questions.q: Nuclear fission of a large nucleus releases energy because the products have:
questions.explain: The fragments lie nearer the peak of the curve with higher binding energy per nucleon, releasing energy.

questions.q: The fact that R is proportional to A^(1/3) implies that nuclear density is:
questions.explain: Mass is proportional to A and volume to R^3 (i.e. A), so density is roughly constant across nuclei.

questions.q: The charge of an up quark in units of e is:
questions.explain: The up quark carries a charge of +2/3 e.

questions.q: The nucleus with the highest binding energy per nucleon is around:
questions.explain: Iron-56 sits near the peak of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve, the most stable region.

questions.q: A 1000 kg car at 20 m s⁻¹ collides and sticks to a stationary 1000 kg car. Their common velocity afterwards is:
questions.explain: By momentum conservation, 1000×20 = 2000×v, so v = 10 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: On the N-Z stability graph, light stable nuclei lie:
options: close to the N = Z line
questions.explain: Light stable nuclei lie near N = Z; heavier ones need more neutrons (curve above the line).

questions.q: In the equation E = mc^2, the c^2 emphasises that a small mass corresponds to:
questions.explain: Because c^2 is enormous, even a tiny mass defect releases a very large amount of energy.

questions.q: Radioactive decay is described as random and spontaneous, meaning it:
options: is unaffected by external conditions like temperature
always occurs at a fixed time
can be predicted for individual nuclei
questions.explain: Decay is spontaneous (unaffected by external factors) and random (unpredictable for a single nucleus).

questions.q: The work done by a constant force is given by:
questions.explain: Work equals force times displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cosθ.

questions.q: Which quantity is conserved in every collision in an isolated system?
questions.explain: Total linear momentum is always conserved when no external resultant force acts.

questions.q: The minimum photon energy needed to produce an electron-positron pair is closest to:
questions.explain: Each particle has rest energy 0.511 MeV, so the minimum is 2 x 0.511 = 1.02 MeV.

questions.q: The impulse of a force is equal to:
questions.explain: Impulse FΔt equals the change in momentum Δp.

questions.q: In beta-plus decay the exchange particle emitted is a:
questions.explain: Beta-plus decay (p -> n) proceeds via emission of a W+ boson.

questions.q: Newton's second law is most fundamentally expressed as:
questions.explain: Force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = Δp/Δt; F = ma is the special case of constant mass.

questions.q: A meson is composed of:
questions.explain: Mesons consist of one quark and one antiquark.

questions.q: In beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a:
questions.explain: n -> p + e- + electron antineutrino.
